newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Feb 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Feb 3.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- HEARTS TAKE THE FIELD FOR FLOTATION

Scottish premier league football club Heart of Midlothian is planning a stock market flotation likely to value the club at between 15 and 20 million pounds stg. Hearts is hoping to raise about 6 million pounds from institutional shareholders, to be spent on ground improvements, debt reduction and renewal of its broadcasting deal with BSkyB.
-- SMALL FIRMS SET THE PACE WITH RISE IN ORDERS

A survey by the Confederation of British Industry says that small firms have boomed during the last four months, with increasing orders and expanding workforces. Their performances are well ahead of larger companies, especially in the home markets, although the export market was an area of concern after the 9 per cent rise in sterling between October and January.
-- CITY WARNS CLARKE OVER VAT

The City of London has warned Chancellor Kenneth Clarke that proposals to impose VAT on property could result in financial institutions locating abroad. The Corporation of London, along with the property profession and landlords, has been fighting the measure, introduced in the Budget last November. Unlike trading organisations, financial companies, which occupy most City properties, cannot recover VAT.
THE TIMES
-- BRUSSELS CLAIMS TORY POLICY ON JOBS FUELLED INEQUALITY

The European Commission has attacked the Tory government's jobs policy, recommending that Britain should reverse major aspects of Conservative employment legislation. The Commission's report on jobs in Britain published today finds that unemployment is likely to fall to a sustainable level of 5 per cent by 2000 but this will have very little to do with government policy, which has led to much greater inequality.
-- C&W TO ABANDON GERMAN ALLIANCE

Cable and Wireless has told its partners that it plans to abandon its German alliance with Vebacom, its partnership with Veba and RWE. The move seems to be the first step in overhauling its international presence under new chief executive, Dick Brown. The company has become increasingly concerned about the cost of competing with Deutsche Telekom.
-- BAA CUTS STAKE IN AIRPORT BID

BAA has reduced its stake in a consortium bidding for Australia's airports. The reduction from 49 to 29 per cent follows fears that being a foreign company could jeopardise its chances. The last minute change came as BAA, along with AMP and Axiom, the Australian fund managers, lodged bids for three Australian airports being sold by the Australian government.
THE GUARDIAN
-- HURDLE FOR EURO IS RAISED BY FAULTY FIGURES

Eurostat, the official statistics arm of the European Commission, will later this month report that some countries aiming to join the single currency in 1999 exaggerate their inflation and output figures, two of the key factors to be used to judge entry. Eurostat plans to call for revision in the way the figures are calculated.
-- CLARKE FORCED TO THE MARGINS OVER DELAY IN SINGLE CURRENCY START-DATE

Britain's isolation in Europe over the proposed start date for the single currency was highlighted in the weekend when supporters of the 1999 date quashed Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's concerns over the timetable. Speaking at the World Economic Forum, the Chancellor expressed doubts the date would be met, but Commission president Jacques Santer said there was no question of a delay.
-- CALL FOR AN INQUIRY INTO MOBILE PHONE PRICING

The Labour party has called for an Office of Fair Trading investigation into a possible cartel or collusion between mobile phone operators Orange and One 2 One. He is concerned that both companies appear to have chosen the same time to seek an increase in their charges to British Telecom for handling calls to their networks, and that the agreed rates are very similar. Both companies deny the allegations.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- SCOTAM SCORNS 'STOP THE CLOCK' PLEA

Scottish Amicable has rejected a demand from Abbey National that it should postpone its controversial plans to end its mutual status. The demand from Abbey follows Scottish Amicable's rejection of the banking group's 1.4 billion pounds stg takeover offer, prompting speculation of a bidding rush by rival suitors. Names thrown into the ring include, Prudential and Allianz of Germany.
-- BRITISH GAS 50 POUNDS STG CALL-OUT ANGERS RIVALS

British Gas has entered a new row with rival suppliers over the costs of administering pre-payment meters in poorer households. Suppliers have been asked by British Gas to pay 50 pounds stg for each emergency visit to homes with pre-payment meters. The new charge could net British Gas 5 million pounds stg a year. The Gas Consumers Council has warned that the fee would encourage new entrants into the competitive market to pick the best customers.
-- NATIONWIDE MAY OFFER INTERNET SERVICE

Nationwide Building Society is looking at the possibility of setting itself up as an Internet service provider. The move would challenge existing commercial providers who traditionally control access to the world-wide web. It is considering the option of offering free or cheap access to its members, although it has not ruled out mounting a direct challenge to service providers such as Pipex, Vigin or Demon, offering cheap access to the Internet to all potential clients.
